question: Your support agent extracts fields such as request type and refund amount, and it gives each field a confidence score. Requests above a confidence threshold are resolved automatically through process_refund, and the rest go to escalate_to_human. The team computes its error rate only from human reviews of escalated cases, and that rate stays steady. After a pricing change, a new error pattern in automatically resolved billing disputes goes unnoticed for six weeks. What is the most likely reason the monitoring missed it?

options.text: The confidence threshold was set too high, so reviewers received more escalated cases than they could check carefully, and their review quality dropped.
options.reason: Weaker reviews of escalated cases do not explain the miss. The errors were in auto-resolved cases, which no reviewer saw at all.

options.text: The team reported one overall error rate across all request types, so a drop in accuracy for billing disputes was hidden inside the aggregate figure.
options.reason: Aggregate metrics can mask weak segments, but the measured rate came only from escalated cases. Splitting that rate by type would still never include the auto-resolved billing disputes.

options.text: Reviewers sorted the escalated cases by request type instead of using one pooled queue, so the separate counts for each type hid the overall trend in billing disputes.
options.reason: The guide recommends analyzing results by segment, so sorting by type does not hide problems. The billing dispute errors were also never in the escalated queue.

options.text: The team never reviewed a stratified random sample of the automatically resolved high-confidence cases, so their error rate and new error patterns went unmeasured.
options.reason: The guide calls for ongoing stratified random sampling of high-confidence outputs to measure their error rate and detect novel patterns. Here only escalated cases were reviewed, so the auto-resolved errors were never seen.
